newsitem.title: FRANCE: Thomson Multimedia set for turnaround in 96 - paper.
newsitem.headline: Thomson Multimedia set for turnaround in 96 - paper.

text.p: Thomson Multimedia, the consumer electronics group owned by Thomson SA, is set to break even in the second half of 1996 after a first-half loss, chairman Alain Prestat told afternoon daily Le Monde in an interview.
He said that one billion francs ($196 million) per year in additional licence income following its 1987 acquisition of RCA meant it would be automatically profitable from 1998.
At the time, Thomson gave seller General Electric the right to licence fees for 10 years, a move which cut the acquisition price.
Prestat said that Thomson Multimedia made a six month net loss of 2.8 billion francs, half of it due to provisions.

"The first half is totally insignificant. The proof is that in the second half of 1996 we will have an operating income which will be largely positive and maybe even a net result at break-even," he said.
He said the first-half loss was due to a new restructuring programme, following one conducted over the 1992 to 1995 period, which was necessery due to a market drop.
"The market crises which we experienced for a year made it indispensable to launch a second plan, which we did in real-time, as Philips is doing now, by taking provisions in the first half.

"Even if 1996 will be known as one of the worst years for consumer products ever, the dynamism remains," Prestat said, adding that after a recapitalisation to cut debts and the licence fees, Thomson Multimedia would be profitable.
Prestat declined to comment on the government's preference to sell Thomson SA for one franc, after an 11 billion franc capital injection, to Lagardere Groupe.
Lagardere Groupe will in turn sell Thomson Multimedia to Daewoo Electronics.
France's Privatisation Commission is expected to announce its decision whether the deal can go ahead in early December.
Prestat said Thomson would make two million digital television decoders in 1996 and expected to make four million by 1998.
